Growing degree-day methods

Source: vignettes/gdd-methods.Rmd
gdd-methods.Rmd

One framework for all daily methods

For an idealised diurnal profile between TminT_{min} and TmaxT_{max}, define

  • the excess I(x)=1P∫0Pmax⁡(0,T(t)−x)dtI(x) = \frac{1}{P}\int_0^P \max(0, T(t) - x)\,dt, and
  • the exceedance F(x)F(x), the fraction of the day with T(t)>xT(t) > x.

Both depend only on the distribution of temperatures within the day. For a sine wave with mean MM and amplitude AA, with θ=arcsin⁡((x−M)/A)\theta = \arcsin((x - M)/A),

I(x)=1π[(M−x)(π2−θ)+Acosθ],F(x)=12−θπ, I(x) = \frac{1}{\pi}\left[(M - x)\left(\frac{\pi}{2} - \theta\right) + A\cos\theta\right], \qquad F(x) = \frac{1}{2} - \frac{\theta}{\pi},

which is the Baskerville-Emin (1969) formula. For a symmetric triangle I(x)=(Tmax−x)2/(2(Tmax−Tmin))I(x) = (T_{max} - x)^2 / (2(T_{max} - T_{min})) when Tmin<x<TmaxT_{min} < x < T_{max}.

With a lower threshold LL and an upper threshold UU:

Cutoff Degree-days Development above UU
none I(L)I(L) unbounded
horizontal I(L)−I(U)I(L) - I(U) constant at U−LU - L
vertical I(L)−I(U)−(U−L)F(U)I(L) - I(U) - (U - L)F(U) zero
intermediate I(L)−2I(U)+I(2U−L)I(L) - 2I(U) + I(2U - L) decreases with slope -1

Double methods split the day into a rising half (Tmin,d→Tmax,dT_{min,d} \to T_{max,d}) and a falling half (Tmax,d→Tmin,d+1T_{max,d} \to T_{min,d+1}), each contributing half a day.

Methods compared 

tmin <- 8; tmax <- seq(10, 40, by = 1)
methods <- c("average", "modified_average", "single_sine", "single_triangle")
cols <- c("grey40", "#8E5BA8", "#0B5563", "#E8702A")
gdd <- sapply(methods, function(m) degree_days(rep(tmin, length(tmax)), tmax,
                                               method = m, base = 10))
matplot(tmax, gdd, type = "l", lty = 1, lwd = 2, col = cols,
        xlab = "Tmax (degC), Tmin = 8 degC", ylab = "GDD base 10 (degC day)")
legend("topleft", legend = methods, lty = 1, lwd = 2, bty = "n", col = cols)

When Tmin<Tb<TmaxT_{min} < T_b < T_{max} the averaging method underestimates heat accumulation because it ignores the warm hours (a consequence of Jensen’s inequality for the convex function max⁡(0,T−Tb)\max(0, T - T_b)).

The modified average (McMaster & Wilhelm 1997, method 2) raises TminT_{min} to TbT_b and caps TmaxT_{max} at TuT_u before averaging. It counts part of the warm hours on cool days, but it is not an integral of the diurnal profile: with Tmin<TbT_{min} < T_b it lies above the averaging method and, in this example, also above the sine and triangle methods, because replacing TminT_{min} by TbT_b assigns the base temperature to the whole cool part of the day. It is the standard method for maize in the United States (Tb=10T_b = 10, Tu=30T_u = 30 degrees C, the “86/50” rule).

Cutoffs are not interchangeable 

tmax <- seq(20, 45, by = 1)
cuts <- c("horizontal", "intermediate", "vertical")
gdd <- sapply(cuts, function(k) degree_days(rep(15, length(tmax)), tmax,
                                            base = 10, upper = 30, cutoff = k))
matplot(tmax, gdd, type = "l", lty = 1, lwd = 2,
        col = c("#0B5563", "#5DA9C9", "#E8702A"),
        xlab = "Tmax (degC), Tmin = 15 degC",
        ylab = "GDD (degC day), base 10, upper 30")
legend("topleft", legend = cuts, lty = 1, lwd = 2, bty = "n",
       col = c("#0B5563", "#5DA9C9", "#E8702A"))

Hourly data

With hourly observations use degree_hours(); the conversion to degree-days divides the daily sum by 24:

temp <- 12 + 9 * sin(2 * pi * (0:47 - 9) / 24)
degree_hours(temp, base = 10, by_day = TRUE)
#> [1] 3.931741 3.931741

Which method?

The differences above are exact consequences of each formula. Which method is closest to the truth depends on the shape of the real diurnal cycle, so on the climate, and on the data available (hourly, daily or monthly).

  • Observed data, semi-arid north-central Chile (30 CEAZA-Met stations, validation article): with daily extremes every method overestimates, because long cool nights put the daily mid-range above the true mean. The averaging method (+5.4 %) and the Linvill reconstruction (gdd_methods = "hourly", +6.0 %, lowest absolute error) are the closest; triangle +7.2 %, sine +8.4 %, modified average +12.2 % (base 10 degrees C, heat season).
  • Synthetic data (article): with a less skewed diurnal cycle the triangle methods and the Linvill reconstruction were within about 1 % and the averaging method underestimated. The observed stations contradict this ranking for semi-arid climates, which shows how strongly the answer depends on the diurnal cycle.

Until the central-south of Chile is validated, use the averaging method or the Linvill reconstruction in dry climates with large diurnal ranges, report which method was used, and treat differences of a few percent between methods as part of the uncertainty. The modified average reproduces a published convention (the “86/50” rule for maize) and should not be used as an estimate of the heat of the day.

Ensembles

No single method is best everywhere, so thermify can combine them. gdd_ensemble_weights() estimates the weights from validate_station() results, that is, from observed hourly records, with three schemes:

  • "stacking" (default): the non-negative weights that sum to one and minimise the squared error. Methods with opposite biases, such as the averaging (too low) and the sine (too high) methods, can be combined.
  • "bma": Bayesian model averaging; weights follow each method’s likelihood.
  • "akaike": Akaike weights, wk∝exp⁡(−ΔAICk/2)w_k \propto \exp(-\Delta AIC_k / 2). The methods have no fitted parameters, so the AIC penalty is the same for all of them and the weights are relative likelihoods: with many seasons they tend to select one method rather than combine several.

BMA and Akaike weights reward the single best method; stacking rewards the best combination. The fitted object reports cross-validated errors (leaving one station out); use the ensemble only when it beats the best single method in cross-validation.

thermify ships no default weights. The weights below are illustrative only:

w <- c(average = 0.4, single_sine = 0.6)   # illustrative, not estimated
gdd_ensemble(c(4, 8, 12), c(18, 24, 31), weights = w, base = 10)
#>    ensemble        sd  min       max average single_sine
#> 1  2.050567 0.8577841  1.0  2.750945     1.0    2.750945
#> 2  6.182410 0.1489372  6.0  6.304017     6.0    6.304017
#> 3 11.500000 0.0000000 11.5 11.500000    11.5   11.500000

gdd_ensemble() returns the members and their spread (sd, min, max) as a measure of method uncertainty. With estimated weights, use degree_days(method = "ensemble", weights = w) or thermify(..., gdd_methods = "ensemble", gdd_weights = w).

References

Baskerville & Emin (1969); Lindsey & Newman (1956); Sevacherian et al. (1977); Allen (1976); Zalom et al. (1983); McMaster & Wilhelm (1997). Full citations are in ?degree_days.
